Hook: In 1798 a country curate, the Reverend Thomas Malthus, published an essay, without his name on it, on the principle of population. Its argument fits in two sentences. Population, when unchecked, increases in a geometrical ratio. Subsistence increases only in an arithmetical ratio. People multiply, one, two, four, eight, while food grows, one, two, three, four. So whenever living standards rise, more children survive and more people marry, until there are enough mouths to push living standards back down. Misery and vice, in his words, keep the numbers in check.

As a description of every century before his, the theory was good. Here are the real wages of English workers from the thirteenth century to his. They rise and fall, sometimes a long way, but over five hundred years they go nowhere. And here is what happened next. By 2016 real wages were about 17 times their level of 1800. Malthus published in the one country, and in the one generation, in which his theory had just stopped being true.

Act Five is about the long run, and it begins with the oldest question in economics. Why was almost everyone poor for almost all of history, and what changed? What kept nearly everyone near subsistence for thousands of years? Why did the escape begin in north-western Europe, around 1800, and not somewhere else, or earlier? And why, once they were richer, did people choose to have fewer children, the opposite of what Malthus expected?
Economics, Built. Part nineteen: the great escape.

This part opens Act Five, the long run. You'll find when the climb began, then derive the Malthusian model and run it. You'll test it on seven centuries of English wages, and watch the Black Death run Malthus's mechanism backwards. Then the arguments over why Britain, why the 1760s, and why not China, and a data film of the great divergence. The Industrial Revolution in numbers, the demographic transition, and one model for the whole story. And whether it was good, a dial on growth before the escape, a famous failed forecast, and the frontier of deep roots.
PlayIt: Chapter one. Play it: when did the climb begin?

Before any theory, a guess. Here is an empty axis: England, from 1270 to 2016, and on it, income per head, in pounds of 2013. Five candidates for the moment when it starts to climb for good: A, 1350; B, 1500; C, 1650; D, 1800; E, 1900. Where does the line leave the floor? Pause, and choose.

Here is the answer, from the Bank of England's millennium dataset, which uses Stephen Broadberry and his colleagues' reconstruction of English output. For five centuries the line lies along the floor. Around 1800 it lifts off, and it has not come down: income per head in 2016 was about 12 times its level of 1800. If you chose D, you chose the moment the floor was left behind for good.

A log scale tells more, because on it equal slopes mean equal rates of growth. From 1270 to 1650, income per head grew by about 0.05 percent a year: nothing. From 1650 to 1800, by more than half a percent a year: a slow climb had begun before the Industrial Revolution. From 1800, by more than one percent a year, for two centuries. And wages were slower still: English real wages did not pass their peak of 1450, set after the Black Death, for good until 1874. Something kept them down for four hundred years. Malthus thought he knew what.
Model: The model has two parts. The first is diminishing returns. Land is fixed. Put more people to work on it, and each produces less: income per head, y, equals technology A times land per person to a power beta, here 0.6. So the more people, the lower the income of each: the curve slopes down. The second part is people. When income per head is high, people marry earlier, more children survive, and fewer people die: births rise with income and deaths fall. At one income they balance. Call it subsistence: not starvation, but the standard of living at which the population just replaces itself.

Put the two parts together. If income is above subsistence, births exceed deaths, the population grows, and with less land each, income falls. If income is below, deaths exceed births, the population shrinks, and income rises. Either way the economy returns to the point where income is at subsistence. It is a stable point: the Malthusian trap. Now invent a better plough, raising A by half. The curve shifts up, and for a while everyone is richer. But the population grows until income is back at subsistence, with 1.97 times as many people. Technology buys people, not income.

Agora runs it. The island starts in its trap: income at subsistence, the population steady. In year 100 a plague kills 45 percent of the islanders. The survivors have more land each, and income per head jumps by 43 percent. Then, slowly, the population recovers, and income falls back: half the gap closes in about 58 years. In year 250 a better plough raises output by half. Income jumps by 59 percent, and again drifts back, while the population climbs towards almost twice its old size. In this world nothing that happens to technology or to death can raise living standards for good. Only fewer births could, which is why, in later editions, Malthus urged what he called moral restraint: marrying later.
Tested: The first prediction: more people, lower wages. Here is every decade of England from 1270 to 1860, its population across and its real wage up, both on log scales. Until about 1640 the decades lie along a falling line. Agora fits it: a slope of minus 0.90, with a standard error, allowing for decades that follow one another, of 0.05. One percent more people meant about nine tenths of a percent lower wages. That is Malthus's labour demand curve, and population explains four fifths of the swings in wages. After 1600 the dots climb to the right: more people and higher wages at once. The curve has stopped binding. That is what an escape looks like in the data.

A word on that standard error, because time series need care. Here are the regression's residuals, year by year: what wages did that population does not explain. They wander in long swings. A year's error is correlated with the next year's, at 0.64. So the 371 years are not 371 independent pieces of evidence. The usual formula, even the one robust to unequal variances, treats them as if they were, and gives 0.022. Whitney Newey and Kenneth West's estimator adds the covariances between nearby years, each down-weighted the further apart they are. With ten years of lags, the standard error more than doubles, to 0.050. How many lags is a judgment, so check it: with forty years, the error is larger still, and the slope is still about 13 standard errors from zero. The conclusion does not depend on the choice.

The second prediction is bolder. Better technology should buy people, not income. Quamrul Ashraf and Oded Galor tested it across countries in the years 1 to 1500. Places where farming began earlier, or whose land was better, had far denser populations, but no measurable advantage in income per head. Gregory Clark went further: the average person in 1800, he argued, lived no better than the average hunter-gatherer. That claim is much disputed in its detail. The broad pattern, technology turning into people, is not.
Plague: Chapter four. The Black Death as an experiment.

In the summer of 1348 the plague reached England. Within three years, by the estimates in the Bank of England's dataset, the population fell from about 4.8 million to 2.6 million: 46 percent of the people died. Later outbreaks kept it falling for a century. Nothing else had changed: the land, the tools, the crops. So Malthus's model makes a sharp prediction, and it came true. Real wages rose to about 2.2 times their level of 1348 by 1400, and 2.7 times by 1450. Then the reversal. As the population recovered, reaching about 5.3 million by 1650, wages fell back to where they had been before the plague. The mechanism ran backwards and then forwards again, over three centuries.

The plague also showed who gained and who resisted. Landlords and employers tried to hold wages down by law: the Statute of Labourers of 1351 capped them at their old levels. The cap failed, and in 1381 the Peasants' Revolt rose partly against such rules. For the survivors, the fifteenth century was a golden age of labour, with more meat, more ale and better clothes. In north-western Europe part of the gain stuck: more people lived in towns, married later, and kept wages higher. Nico Voigtländer and Joachim Voth argued that plague, war and towns, the three horsemen of riches, kept Europe richer than its technology alone would allow. But not out of the trap. By 1650, English wages were back to about their level of 1300.
China: For much of history the obvious place for an escape was China. Printing, paper money, gunpowder, the compass, cast iron and a civil service chosen by examination were all Chinese long before they were European. The biochemist Joseph Needham spent his life on the history of Chinese science, and asked why modern science and industry arose in Europe instead. Economists ask the same question about incomes: why did the great divergence between Europe and Asia happen?

Here is what the Maddison Project's historians estimate, on a log scale, in dollars of 2011. Around the year 1000, China and England were about equally poor, near twelve hundred dollars a head. China's estimates rise and fall between about twelve and fifteen hundred dollars for seven centuries, then sink after 1700, while north-western Europe pulls ahead: first Holland, whose golden age peaks around 1600, then Britain. Italy, rich in the Middle Ages, stays where it was: the little divergence, inside Europe. By 1700 Britain is at about 2,412 dollars against China's 1,543. By 1850, about 4,332 against 858: five to one.

How late the divergence came is the heart of the debate. In 2000 Kenneth Pomeranz argued that as late as 1750 the richest part of China, the Yangzi delta, lived about as well as England. What set England apart was luck: coal close to its people, and the land of the New World, which grew the cotton, sugar and timber that England could not. Stephen Broadberry, Hanhui Guan and David Daokui Li rebuilt China's national accounts from its own records, back to the year 980, and concluded that the Yangzi delta fell decisively behind the richest region of Europe around 1700: later than older writers assumed, but earlier than Pomeranz said. Their estimates are still being argued over. The debate is over the date, and with it the cause: a late accident of geography, or a long European lead.
Industrial: Chapter seven. The Industrial Revolution in numbers.

If the machines were so remarkable, the national figures should show it. They barely do. English income per head grew by about a third of a percent a year from 1700 to 1800, and by only 0.19 percent a year from 1800 to 1830, with war against France for much of it. Nicholas Crafts and Knick Harley revised the older, faster estimates down, and concluded that the revolution was in cotton and iron, not yet in the whole economy. Farms and services, where most people worked, changed slowly. Even steam, Crafts later found, added little to growth until after 1830, because engines were few, costly and fuel-hungry for decades. Then, from 1830 to 1870, growth reached 1.17 percent a year, and it has never gone back.

And the workers? Set output per head and real wages to a hundred in 1780 and follow them. By 1840 output per head had risen by about 31 percent; real wages by about 12. This is the England Friedrich Engels described in 1845, in The Condition of the Working Class in England. Robert Allen called the gap Engels's pause: the gains went to profits, which were reinvested in machines and factories. Only after 1840 did wages begin to catch up. The first two generations of the escape were not the ones who enjoyed it.
Transition: The escape had a second half, and it began with death. In England in 1543, life expectancy at birth was about 34 years; in 1850, still only about 43. In Sweden, whose national records go back furthest, it rose from about 32 in 1800 to about 52 by 1900. For the world as a whole it was about 28 in 1800, and 73 in 2023. Those low averages were not because adults died at thirty: most of the deaths were of children. Cleaner water, better food and, later, vaccines brought them down first.

Then births. Swedish women had about four children each in 1891; by 1935, fewer than two. For the whole world, the figure fell from almost five in 1950 to about 2.3 today, close to the replacement level of about two. South Korea went from six to 0.72, the lowest in the world. And Nigeria, still at about four and a half, is where the transition is now under way. First deaths fell, so for a while populations grew fast; then births followed. That is the demographic transition.

Why would richer people choose fewer children? Gary Becker and H. Gregg Lewis proposed in 1973 that parents choose between the quantity of children and their quality. Every child costs time and money, and an educated child costs more. Agora runs the version Oded Galor and David Weil built: when technology changes faster, schooling pays more, because it helps a child cope with change. Above a threshold, parents start to educate, and since each child now costs more, they have fewer. Falling child deaths, women's rising wages, pensions and contraception all pushed the same way.
Unified: Chapter nine. One model for the whole story.

Can one model produce the trap, the escape and the transition? Two ideas make it possible. Michael Kremer argued in 1993 that more people means more potential inventors, so technology improves faster in bigger populations. In a Malthusian world, better technology means more people: a loop. So population growth itself should speed up over thousands of years. It did, until the 1960s, and regions cut off from the rest, like Tasmania, fell behind. Oded Galor and David Weil added the parents' choice from chapter eight.

The parents' problem is small enough to solve on screen. A child costs a parent a fixed amount of time, tau, plus whatever is spent on schooling, e. The child's human capital, h, rises with schooling and is eroded by technological change, g, because a changing world makes old skills obsolete. Parents choose e to get the most human capital per unit of time spent. Solve it, and the answer has a corner. While technology changes slowly, the best schooling is none: have more children instead. Above a threshold, g hat, equal to rho squared tau over one minus rho, schooling starts to pay, and it rises with the pace of change. That corner is the switch in the unified model: fast enough technology turns parents from quantity to quality.

Agora runs a small version, one generation at a time, from the year 1000. For centuries it is Malthusian: income hovers just above subsistence, technology creeps forward, and every gain becomes more people. As the population grows, technology speeds up, until around 1600 income starts to rise faster than the population can catch it: the post-Malthusian take-off, with population growing faster than ever. Faster change makes schooling pay. Parents begin to educate, and fertility, after peaking around 1875, falls towards replacement. From then on, gains go to income per head, not to numbers: modern growth. One set of equations, three eras. The model is a cartoon, its dates set by its parameters, but its order of events is the one history shows.
Good: Incomes rose; did lives get better? One answer is written in bones. A grown man's height records how well he was fed, and how much disease he fought, as a child. British men born in the 1760s averaged about 170 centimetres. Men born in the 1850s, in the crowded industrial towns, averaged about 165.6: shorter, while income per head rose. Dutch and American men shrank too. Only for those born after the 1850s did heights climb, to about 177 centimetres by the 1960s. Height catches what income misses: the cost of the early industrial city.

Historians have argued about this for a century and a half. The optimists point to more goods, far cheaper cloth, and wages that rose after 1840. The pessimists point to crowded towns, child labour, and shorter, sicker lives. Hans-Joachim Voth found that the English also worked longer years, with fewer holidays, and Jan de Vries argued that households worked harder to buy the new goods: an industrious revolution before the industrial one. In the long run there is no contest: life expectancy has risen from about thirty to over seventy, across the world. For the first generations the escape was a hard bargain. For their great-grandchildren, it was the escape.
Dials: Chapter eleven. The Dials: growth before the escape.

This part opens a dial: how fast did English living standards grow in the four centuries before 1700? Three reconstructions, all in the Bank of England's dataset, answer differently. Output per head, built up from farms, workshops and services, grew by about 0.19 percent a year: enough to double in about 367 years. Real wages from daily wage rates grew by about 0.07 percent: a doubling every thousand years. Count the extra days people worked each year, as Jane Humphries and Jacob Weisdorf did, and earnings grew by about 0.10 percent. The status: contested. The gap is the debate over whether England was already escaping slowly, or stuck until about 1800. The dial returns in part forty-six.

Numbers this small are hard to feel, so compound them. A rough rule: anything growing at g percent a year doubles in about seventy divided by g years. At 0.07 percent, the day wages' rate, four centuries leave living standards only 1.33 times as high: a third better off, in sixteen generations. Counting the extra days worked, 1.52 times. Output per head, at 0.19 percent, more than doubles. The disagreement is between a world that barely moved and one that was slowly getting richer. Either way, it is nothing like the doubling every sixty years or so that began around 1800.

Why such a spread? A day's wage is not a year's income: people worked more days a year as time went on, so day wages understate the gain. Output per head counts everyone, landlords and merchants as well as labourers, whose share may have fallen. The price indexes for the fourteenth century rest on a handful of goods. And the dates matter: 1300 was a crowded, poor moment, so growth measured from it looks faster.
Practice: Chapter twelve. In practice: forecasting the long run.

Called it? In 1968, with the world's population at about 3.5 billion and growing by about 2 percent a year, the biologist Paul Ehrlich opened The Population Bomb with a prediction: the battle to feed all of humanity is over, and in the 1970s hundreds of millions of people will starve to death. The world's population passed 8 billion in 2022, and food per person rose. The famines since, terrible as they were, killed far fewer, and most were made by war and policy rather than by a world short of food. Wrong. It was Malthus's arithmetic, applied just as fertility began to fall and crop yields began to soar.

The economists answered with a bet. In 1980 Julian Simon offered one, and Ehrlich accepted. Ehrlich and two colleagues chose five metals: chromium, copper, nickel, tin and tungsten. They notionally bought a thousand dollars' worth at 1980 prices. If, after inflation, the metals were dearer in 1990, Ehrlich would win. All five fell, and in 1990 Ehrlich mailed Simon a cheque for five hundred and seventy-six dollars and seven cents. Economists later found that over many other decades Ehrlich would have won: metal prices swing with booms and busts. The lesson is not that scarcity never bites, but that prices call forth substitutes and new supplies, on no fixed timetable.

Long-run forecasting is now routine work. The United Nations' projections of 2024 have the world's population peaking at about 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s, then slowly declining. Sixty-three countries are already past their peak, among them China, Germany, Japan and Russia. Treasuries and pension funds plan on projections fifty years out, and climate models take paths of population and income as their inputs, as part forty-eight shows. The demographic transition, not the bomb, is now the central forecast.
Frontier: Chapter thirteen. Frontier: deep roots and persistence.

The frontier asks how deep the roots of the escape go. If it spread out from north-western Europe, who caught it first, and why? Diego Comin, William Easterly and Erick Gong found that the technologies a region used in 1500, and even in 1000 BC, predict its income today. Enrico Spolaore and Romain Wacziarg found that populations more distant in ancestry from the leaders adopted new ideas later, and read it as a barrier of language and custom to the spread of know-how, not as anything in the genes themselves. Quamrul Ashraf and Oded Galor went further, relating a country's genetic diversity to its income. That paper was sharply criticized by anthropologists and geneticists for what such data can and cannot mean.

There is also a warning about method. Morgan Kelly noticed that many persistence studies regress one map on another: a medieval pattern against a modern one. Nearby places resemble each other, in both. Agora shows what that does. Take 300 places, draw two random maps that have nothing to do with each other, regress one on the other, and repeat 400 times. If the maps have no spatial pattern, about 5 percent of the regressions look significant, as they should. If each map varies smoothly over space, like most real ones, about 55 percent do. Nearby places are not independent pieces of evidence, and standard errors that pretend they are can find deep roots in pure noise.

Some questions remain open. Was the escape inevitable once ideas could spread, or an accident of one island? How much did empire, slavery and colonial trade contribute to it? Can poor countries repeat it faster today, and with what? Part forty-six takes that up. And if more people meant more ideas, what happens to growth when populations begin to shrink?
Outro: So: why was almost everyone poor for almost all of history, and what changed? Because in a world of fixed land, every gain in technology turned into more people rather than more income. That was Malthus's trap, and England's wages obeyed it for five centuries. What changed was that technology began to improve faster than population could catch it, and then that parents, in a world where skills paid, chose fewer, better-educated children. Why it began in north-western Europe, around 1800, is still argued: prices, ideas and institutions all played a part.

Part nineteen in twelve lines. Malthus argued that population grows geometrically and food only arithmetically. In Play it, England's income per head left the floor around 1800, and has multiplied about 12 times since. The model joins diminishing returns to a population that follows income, and has a stable trap. England's wages obeyed it: one percent more people meant about 0.9 percent lower wages until about 1640. The Black Death killed 46 percent of the English, and wages rose almost threefold before falling back. Britain went first, for reasons of prices, ideas and institutions that are still argued over, and the new national accounts date China's fall behind to around 1700. Growth was slow until 1830, and wages lagged. Deaths fell first, then births. One model, with a scale effect and the choice between quantity and quality, produces three eras. Heights fell for two generations before the escape paid. And a dial on growth before the escape, Ehrlich's bomb, and deep roots that may be spatial noise.

The problems. The Malthusian steady state; the plague's jump and its half-life; England's labour demand curve; growth rates and doubling times; Engels's pause; the quantity-quality threshold; Kremer's scale effect; and a starred problem on spatial noise. Full solutions are in the part's notes.

The reading: Gregory Clark's A Farewell to Alms, for the Malthusian view at its boldest; Robert Allen's British Industrial Revolution in Global Perspective, for prices; Joel Mokyr's A Culture of Growth, for ideas; Oded Galor's Unified Growth Theory, and Kenneth Pomeranz's The Great Divergence. Then the papers, from Malthus to spatial noise.

This part asked how the escape began. The next asks what sustains it. In 1956 Robert Solow wrote down one equation for what saving and capital can do, and what they cannot. Part twenty: growth, and capital.
